paras.text: Takao to Manila, sailed 1300 on 28 April 1944 (the escort division's table). Only one ship's cargo is recorded: Nittatsu Maru loaded 250 t of coal at Takao to be landed at Manila (her master's log, p23). The other ships' cargoes and the convoy's arrival are not in the records read. BANG attacked it on 29–30 April; PARCHE and TINOSA were in the same fight against two convoys (engagement `luzon-strait-1944`, which says which boat attacked which).

The retired battle page listed thirteen merchant ships from combinedfleet.com. Ten are on combinedfleet's page for Nittatsu Maru (28 April: Kennichi, Kurogane, Belgium, Peking, Shiroganesan, Takegawa, Tsushima, San Luis, Wales, Yamahagi and Shirotae Maru, escorted by Harukaze, W-17 and the auxiliary gunboat Chohakusan Maru; Asakaze joined on the 29th), and are in `ships:` as secondary. Its Nissan Maru, and the Yashima and Hakka Maru that "other lists add", are on no page found, so they are left out. combinedfleet's Chohakusan Maru is the escort division table's Chojusan Maru (as read).

paras.text: Yulin to Moji, leaving Yulin on 30 April 1944 with six ships (April chart). The May chart draws the northbound track with two sinking marks and lists five ships sunk: 金嶺丸 昌竜丸 大翼丸 豊日丸 大武丸; the rest of the convoy is drawn into (基隆) Keelung for supplies (補給) and on to Moji. Six ships less five sunk leaves one survivor (inferred).

The chart's time and position beside the marks are faint: read 「4日 22?9」 N2?-46 E118-?4, low confidence; not paired with any one boat's attack. BANG, PARCHE and TINOSA attacked between the evening of the 3rd and the early hours of the 4th (engagement `luzon-strait-1944`, which weighs who sank which).
**Cargo: iron ore for Yawata** per combinedfleet.com (secondary); not in the escort division's record. The escorts are combinedfleet's; the April chart's escort cell can't be read with confidence.
The retired battle page listed a sixth ship, "Yulin", from combinedfleet.com; that is the port of departure, not a ship, and is left out. The sixth ship (the survivor) is not named in the record.

paras.text: Moji to Singapore by way of Manila, June–July 1944. The escort division's June chart starts the track in the 22 June column (Kurahashi joined from Sasebo that day: combinedfleet:Kurahashi_t, secondary); the sailing date of 20 June is combinedfleet.com's (secondary). The July chart has the convoy leave Manila on the 3rd with 7 ships and reach 昭南 on the 9th.

**Cargo: not recorded** in any record read. The southbound HI convoys took oilers to Singapore to load (inferred, not from a record of this convoy). Miri Maru's designated-ship log (jacar:C08050103600 p21–25) ends on 10 June 1944, when the Navy took her over, so it stops before this voyage. Gokoku, Asahisan, Miri and Sarawak Maru left the convoy at Manila (combinedfleet, secondary).

**Why the tankers mattered** (context, secondary: wolborsky, a 1994 Air University thesis drawing on the Strategic Bombing Survey). In the fall of 1943 the Navy made tankers its submarines' first target, and early in 1944 it decided to put submarines in the Luzon Strait, "astride the main Japanese oil lifeline" (wolborsky/p20). BANG met HI-67 west of Luzon, at 17-13N 118-22E, on that same route south (inference from the convoy's track). Japan's tanker fleet peaked at 834,000 tons in November 1943; once the attacks focused on oil, monthly tanker sinkings tripled, and oil imports to the home islands fell from a peak of 1.75 million barrels in August 1943 to 300,000 barrels a month by October 1944 (wolborsky/p28). Of the 28.5 million barrels Japan expected to import in 1944 it received 4,975,000 (the Survey, quoted at wolborsky/p33). None of this is HI-67's own record: BANG's hit on Miri and Sarawak Maru did minor damage to both, and neither was lost on this voyage.

convoys.cargo: anti-aircraft guns and ammunition in Gyoun Maru (secondary); the rest not recorded

ships.note: Destroyer. Named as escort (護衛艦栗) of 第九一船団 on 4 July; sent the convoy's reports in the submarine table (p28)
Torpedo boat. Named as escort (初雁) of 第九一船団 on 4 July; at 1055 reported a periscope sighted and attacked, oil brought up (p28)
日東丸. In the convoy by inference: Kuri reported her sinking, and the narrative (p27) puts 第九一船団 under attack that day
暁勇丸. In the convoy by inference, as Nitto Maru
第二八共同丸. In the convoy by inference, as Nitto Maru

Also read Agekumo Maru; ex Ethel Moller, 912 GRT (the comment). The post summarises a BAAG report: arrived Hong Kong from Shanghai via Formosa, inward cargo anti-aircraft guns and ammunition, discharged 21-22 July to the Tsim Sha Tsui barracks; it dates the arrival 20 July. A reader's comment (P. Cundall, 4 Dec 2018, no source cited) puts her in TA-406 Shanghai to Takao and then No. 91 Takao to Hong Kong with Nitto, Kyodo No. 28 and Gyoyu Maru, the only one of four to survive, arriving 5 July. Not yet in a Japanese record

paras.text: Attacked southwest of Pratas Island (東沙島) on 4 July 1944; the diary estimated two or three submarines. SEAHORSE's attacks pair with Kuri's two sinking reports by time and place; BANG's with Kuri's 0515 "no damage" report by time alone (inferred). **Ports, cargo and the number of ships are not recorded** in the 2nd China Expeditionary Fleet diary. "To Hong Kong" is inferred from the course on SEAHORSE's attack sheets (270, then 320–335) and the escorts, which were Hong Kong's (Kuri and Hatsukari escort another convoy off 碣石湾 on 29 July, p26). SEAHORSE counted five freighters and two destroyers with other escorts.

A secondary account fills in the route: a reader's comment on the Industrial History of Hong Kong post about Gyoun Maru (industrialhistoryhk:29957, no source cited) says four ships came from Shanghai to Takao as TA-406 and went on to Hong Kong as No. 91, and that Gyoun Maru alone survived, reaching Hong Kong on 5 July. The post's BAAG summary has her inward cargo as anti-aircraft guns and ammunition (but an arrival date of 20 July). Four ships agrees with three sunk and one surviving; SEAHORSE counted five freighters.
To find: a Japanese record of the sailing port (Takao, Manila or Yulin), and whether Nitto, Gyoyu or No. 28 Kyodo Maru has a movement log with her cargo.

paras.text: The Japanese record of the loss is the Yokosuka Guard Squadron's September diary (p3): 昌隆丸 (Shoryu Maru) and 常盤山丸 (Tokiwasan Maru) torpedoed and sunk at 1520 on the 9th, four minutes after BANG's first salvo (1616 K = 1516 I). It gives the place as 265° 10 nm from Sumisu-jima, which is about 188 nm north-east of BANG's attack position; BANG's position agrees with the postwar one combinedfleet gives (28-58N 137-45E). The diary doesn't name the convoy.

The route and escorts are combinedfleet.com's (secondary). It has the convoy leave Yokosuka on 6 September for Haha-jima, reach Tateyama on the 7th, and leave Tateyama "at 1520" on the 9th, then be attacked "at about 1600" at 28-58N 137-45E. That can't be right: Tateyama is about 360 nm north of that position, and 1520 on the 9th is the diary's time of the sinking. The Tateyama sailing was probably the 7th or 8th (inferred, to check). The escort grid (p5) fits Yasojima (父島 across about days 8–11) but has CD-4 at Yokosuka and Tateyama until about the 10th; all read with low confidence from a skewed scan.
**Cargo: not recorded.** BANG saw one oiler (AO) and two freighters.

paras.text: Attacked by BANG on 19 September 1944 off the north-east coast of Formosa. The Okinawa diary names six escorts and the one ship lost, No. 2 Tosei Maru, and says CD-30 and Taian Maru with army aircraft attacked the submarine and claimed it sunk. BANG surfaced that night after about 80 depth charges.

**Route and size** from the 4th Surface Escort Division's table of convoys given air cover (jacar:C08030144100 p05, read on the image 5 Nov 2026): on the 19th, TAKA-909, ten ships of 34,049 tons, escorted by CD-30, W-15, No. 3 Takunan Maru, Shichiri Maru, Taian Maru and No. 3 Taihei Maru, routed Keelung to Kagoshima and Naha to Kagoshima. So it sailed from Keelung, not Takao as the convoy code had suggested. Its sailing time and cargo are not recorded. The waypoints off Formosa's east coast and Kagoshima Bay are assumed. BANG counted eight merchantmen, one an oiler.

No other US boat's attack on TAKA-909 has been found: the diary's columns for the 18th–21st have only this attack and, on the 20th, an attack on the depot ship Jingei far to the east (N27-12.5 E127-10.0; not BANG's).
To find: TAKA-909's sailing time from Keelung and its ships' names (its escorts' own September diaries).

paras.text: Keelung to Naha, sailing at 0800 on 22 November 1944 with six ships and four escorts (W-15's battle report, p32–33). Three were sunk that night (Hozan, Amakusa and Sakae Maru); the other three sheltered at Funauki (Iriomote) on the 23rd. BANG, REDFISH and SHAD all attacked it (engagement `bang-patrol-4`).
**Cargo: not recorded** in W-15's report. The table gives each ship a type letter (A or C, not explained on the page), a top speed and a displacement.
